==Scientific accuracy==
{{see also|Effect of spaceflight on the human body|Human mission to Mars|Plants in space}}
[[File:James L Green.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.75|[[James L. Green]], the Director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA's [[Science Mission Directorate]], worked as an adviser for the film.<ref name="ordona">{{cite news | last=Ordoña | first=Michael | url=http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Will-Matt-Damon-be-our-new-favorite-Martian-6469122.php | title=Will Matt Damon be our new favorite Martian? | work=[[San Francisco Chronicle]] | date=August 27, 2015 | access-date=September 1, 2015 | archive-date=September 1, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150901202850/http://www.sfgate.com/movies/article/Will-Matt-Damon-be-our-new-favorite-Martian-6469122.php | url-status=live }}</ref>]]
When Weir wrote the novel ''The Martian'', he strove to present the science correctly and used reader feedback to get it right.<ref name="cohn">{{cite news | last=Cohn | first=Paulette | url=https://www.foxnews.com/science/the-science-behind-the-martian-movie-gets-a-nasa-thumbs-up/ | title=The science behind 'The Martian' movie gets a NASA 'thumbs up' | publisher=[[Fox News Channel]] | date=August 28, 2015 | access-date=September 1, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150831080557/http://www.foxnews.com/science/2015/08/28/science-behind-martian-movie-gets-nasa-thumbs-up/ | archive-date=August 31, 2015 | url-status=live | df=mdy-all }}</ref> When Scott began directing the film, he also sought to make it realistic and received help from [[James L. Green]], the Director of the Planetary Science Division at NASA's [[Science Mission Directorate]]. Green put together teams to answer scientific questions that Scott asked.<ref name="french">{{cite news | last1=French | first1=Francis | last2=Pearlman | first2=Robert | url=https://www.csmonitor.com/Science/Science-Notebook/2015/0906/NASA-and-The-Martian-partner-to-make-space-cool-and-accurate | title=NASA and 'The Martian' partner to make space 'cool' – and accurate | work=[[The Christian Science Monitor]] | date=September 6, 2015 | access-date=October 2, 2015 | archive-date=October 3, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003122600/http://www.csmonitor.com/Science/Science-Notebook/2015/0906/NASA-and-The-Martian-partner-to-make-space-cool-and-accurate | url-status=live }}</ref> Green said, "''The Martian'' is reasonably realistic", though he said the film's hazardous dust storm, despite reaching speeds of {{convert|120|mph|kph}}, would in reality have weak force.<ref>{{cite news | last=Dorminey | first=Bruce | url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucedorminey/2015/08/31/rethinking-the-martian-why-dust-storms-wouldnt-sabotage-a-real-mars-mission/ | title=Rethinking 'The Martian': Why Dust Storms Wouldn't Sabotage A Real Mars Mission | work=[[Forbes]] | date=August 31, 2015 | access-date=September 1, 2015 | archive-date=September 4, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150904010414/http://www.forbes.com/sites/brucedorminey/2015/08/31/rethinking-the-martian-why-dust-storms-wouldnt-sabotage-a-real-mars-mission/ | url-status=live }}</ref> Green also found the NASA buildings in the film to be more stylish than the [[Functionalism (architecture)|functional]] ones NASA actually uses.<ref>{{cite news | last=Schwartz | first=John | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/13/movies/the-martian-author-andy-weir-brings-his-nerd-thriller-into-the-mainstream.html | title='The Martian' Brings a Nerd Thriller Into the Mainstream | work=[[The New York Times]] | date=September 9, 2015 | access-date=October 2, 2015 | archive-date=October 1, 2015 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001003000/http://www.nytimes.com/2015/09/13/movies/the-martian-author-andy-weir-brings-his-nerd-thriller-into-the-mainstream.html | url-status=live }}</ref> Film critics picked up the point that the Martian winds could amount to "barely a light breeze" in their reviews,<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.theguardian.com/film/2015/sep/20/space-experts-the-martian-matt-damon|title=Space experts challenge accuracy of The Martian|first=Jamie|last=Grierson|work=The Guardian|date=September 20, 2015|access-date=October 3, 2015|archive-date=October 1, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151001222439/http://www.theguardian.com/film/2015/sep/20/space-experts-the-martian-matt-damon|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://news.discovery.com/space/space-experts-swoon-for-the-martian-despite-inaccuracies-150925.htm|title=Space experts swoon for 'The Martian' despite inaccuracies|first=Kerry|last=Sheridan|work=DNews |publisher=Discovery|date=September 25, 2015|access-date=October 3, 2015|archive-date=October 4, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151004213434/http://news.discovery.com/space/space-experts-swoon-for-the-martian-despite-inaccuracies-150925.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> and screenwriter Goddard agreed the winds had to be considerably exaggerated to set up the situation that sets the story in motion.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Martian screenwriter admits his film has one major scientific inaccuracy |first=Huw |last=Fullerton |work=Radio Times |date=October 1, 2015 |url=http://www.radiotimes.com/news/2015-10-01/the-martian-screenwriter-admits-his-film-has-one-major-scientific-inaccuracy |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151004040927/http://www.radiotimes.com/news/2015-10-01/the-martian-screenwriter-admits-his-film-has-one-major-scientific-inaccuracy |archive-date=October 4, 2015 |access-date=March 1, 2021 }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://time.com/4055413/martian-movie-review-science-accuracy-matt-damon/|title=What The Martian gets right (and wrong) about science|first=Jeffrey|last=Kluger|magazine=Time|date=September 30, 2015|access-date=October 3, 2015|archive-date=October 3, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003014539/http://time.com/4055413/martian-movie-review-science-accuracy-matt-damon/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.iflscience.com/space/how-accurate-martian-9-things-movie-got-right-and-wrong|title=How accurate is The Martian?|first=Jonathan|last=O'Callaghan|publisher=I Fucking Love Science|date=September 30, 2015|access-date=October 3, 2015|archive-date=October 3, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003000152/http://www.iflscience.com/space/how-accurate-martian-9-things-movie-got-right-and-wrong|url-status=live}}</ref>

The process used by the character Watney to produce water is chemically accurate and theoretically possible. The [[radioisotope thermoelectric generator]] was also appropriately used for heat.<ref name="cohn" /> When his rations begin to run low, Watney builds an improvised [[Plants in space|garden]] using [[Martian soil]] and the crew's [[Human feces|feces]] as a fertilizer. However, [[Martian soil]] has since been found to be [[Martian soil#Toxicity|toxic]] to both plant and animal life, although it is believed that [[Life on Mars|microbial organisms have the potential to live on Mars]].<ref name="toxicsoil1">{{cite web |title=Mars covered in toxic chemicals that can wipe out living organisms, tests reveal |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/jul/06/mars-covered-in-toxic-chemicals-that-can-wipe-out-living-organisms-tests-reveal |website=The Guardian |date=July 6, 2017 |access-date=November 26, 2018 |archive-date=December 3, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181203175249/https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/jul/06/mars-covered-in-toxic-chemicals-that-can-wipe-out-living-organisms-tests-reveal |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="toxicmars">{{cite web |title=Toxic Mars: Astronauts Must Deal with Perchlorate on the Red Planet |url=https://www.space.com/21554-mars-toxic-perchlorate-chemicals.html |website=space.com |date=June 13, 2013 |access-date=November 26, 2018 |archive-date=November 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201120151522/https://www.space.com/21554-mars-toxic-perchlorate-chemicals.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |last=Twilley |first=Nicola |title=Meet the Martians |url=https://www.newyorker.com/tech/elements/meet-the-martians |access-date=May 30, 2016 |magazine=The New Yorker |date=October 8, 2015 |archive-date=May 11, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160511230930/http://www.newyorker.com/tech/elements/meet-the-martians |url-status=live }}</ref>

[[Jeffrey Kluger]] of [[Time (magazine)|''Time'']] magazine criticized a depiction of duct tape based repair: "When a pressure leak causes an entire pod on Watney's habitat to blow up, he patches a yawning opening in what's left of the dwelling with plastic tarp and PSA duct tape." Such a repair would not work in an average Martian temperature of {{convert|-60|C}}.<ref name="time-off" />

While Martian gravity is less than 40% of Earth's, director Scott chose not to depict the gravitational difference, finding the effort less worthwhile to put on screen than zero gravity.<ref name="bradley" /> Scott said the heavy spacesuits would weigh the main character enough to make up for not showing the partial gravity.<ref name="dave" /> <!--Find sources and edit the content that appears here, to them. Per WP:VERIFY, veracity here is based on traceability to source. This is not a 6th form student essay:  The [[climate of Mars]] is also cold enough that it would make Watney's initial plan to disable the rover's heater immediately impractical, since the average temperature is {{convert|-80|F|C}}; it is cold enough on Mars for [[carbon dioxide]] snow to fall at the poles in winter.{{citation needed|date=April 2021}} However, this issue is almost immediately brought up, and is the reason for the plan failing.-->[[File:The route of 'The Martian' - from Chryse Planitia over Arabia Terra in the Martian highlands to Ares 4.jpg|thumb|300px|Mark Watney's route on Mars]]The plot key to the eventual rescue plan is [[gravity assist]], a well-known practice that has been used on a number of robotic planetary exploration missions and served as a backup strategy on crewed Apollo missions. It would have been one of the first approaches that everyone within NASA would have considered.<ref name="time-off">{{cite magazine |date=September 30, 2015 |author=Jeffrey Kluger |url=https://time.com/4055413/martian-movie-review-science-accuracy-matt-damon/ |title=What 'The Martian' Gets Right (and Wrong) About Science |magazine=TIME |access-date=October 3, 2015 |archive-date=October 3, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151003014539/http://time.com/4055413/martian-movie-review-science-accuracy-matt-damon/ |url-status=live }}</ref> <!--Find sources and edit the content that appears here, to them. Per WP:VERIFY, veracity here is based on traceability to source. This is not a 6th form student essay:  (In the film, only one JPL astrodynamicist argues for sending the Ares mission back to Mars using gravity assist rather than having a separate mission to rescue Watney.-->

Ed Finn, director of the Center for Science and the Imagination at [[Arizona State University]], said, "What this story does really well is imagine a near-future scenario that doesn't push too far off where we are today technically."<ref name="dave"/> British physicist [[Brian Cox (physicist)|Brian Cox]] said, "''The Martian'' is the best advert for a career in engineering I've ever seen."<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/77051969/human-universes-brian-cox-anwers-the-big-questions | title=Human Universe's Brian Cox answers the big questions | publisher=[[Stuff.co.nz]] | date=February 22, 2016 | access-date=June 12, 2016 | archive-date=March 24, 2016 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160324164944/http://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/77051969/Human-Universes-Brian-Cox-anwers-the-big-questions | url-status=live }}</ref>
